alt: The same incident, a driver killing a pedestrian, can lead to a negligence claim and a criminal charge, which are separate. A table compares them: the claimant sues in tort but the CPS usually prosecutes; tort uses the balance of probabilities and crime beyond reasonable doubt; tort gives liability and a remedy, crime a conviction and sentence; tort aims at compensation, crime at punishment.
caption: Tort compensates the claimant; crime punishes on behalf of society.

alt: Common law torts built case by case: negligence (Donoghue, Caparo, Robinson), private nuisance (Hunter v Canary Wharf), Rylands v Fletcher (Transco), vicarious liability (Various Claimants, Lister) and consent (Smith v Baker, ICI v Shatwell). Statutory rules: the Occupiers’ Liability Acts 1957 and 1984 and the Contributory Negligence Act 1945. In negligence, established precedent comes first and Caparo is only for novel situations.
caption: Negligence grows case by case; occupiers’ liability starts from the Acts’ wording.

alt: The claimant proves each element of the tort on the balance of probabilities, and the defendant proves any defence. Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington shows a claim failing on causation. Res ipsa loquitur (Scott v London and St Katherine Docks) and a criminal conviction used as evidence under s11 Civil Evidence Act 1968 can help the claimant.
caption: The claimant proves the tort; the defendant proves the defence.

after: ## Liability and fault across the torts
alt: A spectrum from personal fault needed to no personal fault. Negligence is fault-based (Vaughan v Menlove; Bolton v Stone; Paris v Stepney). Occupiers’ liability is a fault-based statutory duty. Private nuisance asks whether use of land was unreasonable (Christie v Davey on malice). Rylands v Fletcher is strict but requires foreseeable damage (Cambridge Water). Vicarious liability requires no personal fault by the employer.
caption: From negligence to vicarious liability, the need for personal fault falls away.

after: ## Defences and remedies as part of the rules
alt: Illustrative bars show full damages with no defence, reduced damages with contributory negligence and nothing with consent. Contributory negligence under the 1945 Act reduces damages by a just share, for example 25% or 15% for not wearing a seat belt (Froom v Butcher). Consent is complete where the claimant knew of and freely agreed to the risk (Smith v Baker; Morris v Murray), but rescuers do not consent (Haynes v Harwood). Nuisance and Rylands have specific defences.
caption: Contributory negligence reduces damages; consent defeats the claim.

alt: Parties: Kit sues Jas in negligence and SpeedyParcels Ltd through vicarious liability. Duty is established (Robinson); breach by using a phone while reversing (Vaughan v Menlove); damage by but for causation (Barnett) and foreseeable harm (Wagon Mound); Jas acted in the course of employment; Kit ignored a warning sign so damages are reduced for contributory negligence, though consent is unlikely.
caption: Identify every party who might pay, then end with defences and remedies.
